name: Aboriginal Australian
line: Know whose Country you are on, listen deeply, move with the seasons and look after the place that looks after you.

quote.text: We cannot hurry the river. We have to move with its current and understand its ways.
quote.source: Dadirri: Inner Deep Listening and Quiet Still Awareness, a reflection first given in 1988. She is an Elder of the Ngan’gityemerri people of the Daly River

quotes.text: We invite you to walk with us in a movement of the Australian people for a better future.
quotes.by: The Uluru Statement from the Heart
quotes.source: The closing line of the statement issued by the First Nations National Constitutional Convention, 26 May 2017

quotes.text: Let no one say the past is dead. The past is all about us and within.
quotes.source: The opening of her poem The Past, 1970
From his Letter from Black to White, 1976. He was a leader of the Gumatj clan of the Yolŋu people

quotes.text: One cannot fix the Dreaming in time: it was, and is, everywhen.
quotes.source: The Dreaming, 1953. An anthropologist’s attempt to put an Aboriginal idea into English

quotes.text: If you have come here to help me, you are wasting your time. But if you have come because your liberation is bound up with mine, then let us work together.
quotes.source: Often credited to Lilla Watson, a Gangulu woman, who asks that it be credited to the group she worked with

words.meaning: The land, waters and sky a person belongs to
words.usage: Much more than scenery or property. Country is family, law and story, and it is spoken of as a living relative. It is written with a capital.

words.meaning: The creation and the law that came from it
words.usage: An imperfect English word for ideas that each language names differently. Ancestral beings shaped the land and laid down how to live, and what they did is still present.

words.meaning: The law and stories of creation
words.usage: The word used by Anangu of the Western Desert. The Warlpiri say Jukurrpa and the Arrernte Altyerre. Each means law, story and the right way of living together.

words.meaning: Past, present and future at once
words.usage: A word coined by the anthropologist W. E. H. Stanner in 1953 to say that the Dreaming is not a time long ago.

words.meaning: A track of an ancestral journey, held in song
words.usage: Routes across the continent marked by places where ancestors acted. The songs carry the map, the law and the knowledge of water and food.

words.meaning: Deep listening and quiet, still awareness
words.usage: A word from the Daly River region, shared with all Australians by the Elder Miriam-Rose Ungunmerr-Baumann. It is a patient, contemplative attention.

words.meaning: Holding; caring with responsibility
words.usage: The principle of connectedness through care. The Elder Bob Randall taught it as four ties: to law, to spirit, to land and to family.

words.meaning: Home; camp; one’s Country
words.usage: The place a person belongs to and is responsible for.

words.meaning: Family; kin
words.usage: Relations in the widest sense, including people, places and other species one is tied to.

words.meaning: In turn; I give and you give
words.usage: Reciprocity. What is given comes back around, and both sides are bound by it.

words.meaning: Respect; to go slowly, be gentle and honour
words.usage: A way of living that is careful, polite and considered. The Elder Stan Grant Senior helped to revive the Wiradjuri language that carries it.

words.meaning: To hear; to listen; to know; to remember
words.usage: One verb for all four. To know something is to have listened.

words.meaning: The system of kinship
words.usage: The Yolŋu web of relationship that places every person, clan, place and animal in a family tie with every other.

words.meaning: Coming together after a struggle
words.usage: A process of peacemaking in which a wrong is faced and settled so that people can live together again. The Uluru Statement asks for one.

words.meaning: Where fresh water and salt water meet
words.usage: The place in a lagoon where two currents mix and foam. Yolŋu teachers use it as a picture of two kinds of knowledge meeting without either being lost.

words.meaning: An open ceremonial ground; a place of two-way learning
words.usage: A place where people of different clans, and now different peoples, meet to share knowledge.

words.meaning: Inner spirit; one’s feeling of wellbeing
words.usage: From Broome. Good liyan comes from right relations with family, community and Country.

words.meaning: One’s people
words.usage: Family, clan or community. Which mob are you is a way of asking where a person belongs.

words.meaning: A senior person who holds knowledge and authority
words.usage: Recognised by the community for wisdom and service, not simply for age.

words.meaning: Respectful titles for older people
words.usage: Used for Elders whether or not they are relatives. It is polite to wait until you are invited to use them.

words.meaning: Talking together; telling stories
words.usage: Unhurried conversation in which people sit as equals and each has a turn. Knowledge is passed on this way.

words.meaning: A person’s place in the kinship system
words.usage: In many communities each person is born into a named group that sets how they relate to everyone else.

words.meaning: A species or thing a person is tied to and must protect
words.usage: An animal, plant or feature of the land inherited through family. Each language has its own word for it.

words.meaning: The customs of mourning
words.usage: The time and duties that follow a death. In many communities the name and image of the person are not used for a period.

words.meaning: A greeting given by Traditional Owners
words.usage: Only the people of that Country can give it. Others may offer an Acknowledgement of Country.

words.meaning: Looking after land and sea as a duty
words.usage: Burning, protecting sites, managing water and species. Indigenous rangers now do this work across almost half the continent.

words.meaning: Small, cool fires lit at the right time
words.usage: Patch burning that clears undergrowth, brings new growth and prevents large wildfires. It has been practised for tens of thousands of years.

words.meaning: Native foods
words.usage: Seeds, fruits, roots, game and fish gathered and prepared with detailed knowledge of season and place.

words.meaning: Excellent
words.usage: The highest praise.

words.meaning: Good; fine; hello
words.usage: A greeting, a thank you and a word of agreement in the Western Desert.

practices.name: Dadirri: deep listening
practices.instructions: Go outside, or sit by an open window, and be still for fifteen minutes. There is nothing to achieve. Do not try to empty your mind and do not look for anything. Listen to what is around you: wind, birds, water, traffic, your own breath. Let it come to you. The rule of this Onda is to listen before you speak.
practices.why: Dadirri, inner deep listening and quiet still awareness, is a gift from the Ngan’gikurunggurr and Ngen’giwumirri people of the Daly River region, shared with all Australians by Miriam-Rose Ungunmerr-Baumann.
variations: Listen in the same spot each day.
Listen with a friend in silence.

practices.name: Acknowledge Country
practices.instructions: Find out whose land you are standing on. In Australia, learn the name of the Traditional Owners of the place where you live and how to say it. Elsewhere, learn who lived on your land first and whether they are still there. Say aloud, in your own words, that you acknowledge them and their Elders past and present. Mean it. The rule of this Onda is to know whose Country you are on.
practices.why: An Acknowledgement of Country is a respectful statement made by anyone, Aboriginal or not, to recognise the Traditional Owners. A Welcome to Country, by contrast, is given only by Traditional Owners.
variations: Look up the Traditional Owners on a map.
Find the name of a local Elder who has shared teaching.

practices.name: A word of local language
practices.instructions: Learn one word from the Aboriginal language of the place where you live, from a trusted source such as a local language centre or council. Learn what it means and how to say it. Use it once today, with care. If you are outside Australia, learn a word from the language of the people of your own region. Learning language is a way of honouring Country.
practices.why: More than 250 Aboriginal languages were spoken in Australia at the time of colonisation, and many are being revived. Learning a word shows respect and interest.
variations: Learn the name of a local bird.
Learn the name for the place where you live.

practices.name: Lemon myrtle tea
practices.instructions: Make a cup of tea from lemon myrtle leaves, a rainforest tree of eastern Australia with a strong lemony fragrance. Steep a few dried leaves or a teabag in hot water and breathe in the steam before you drink. Buy from an Aboriginal-owned supplier if you can. Sip slowly and think of the trees whose leaves are in your cup.
practices.why: Lemon myrtle has been used by Aboriginal people for food and healing for thousands of years. Buying from Aboriginal-owned suppliers supports their economy.
variations: Look at a lemon myrtle tree.

practices.name: Who is calling?
practices.instructions: Listen for the first bird calling in your area at dawn, and find out its name: magpie, kookaburra, butcherbird, wattlebird. Note when it calls and what else is happening. Many Aboriginal peoples read the birds as messengers and seasonal markers. Learn one bird’s call well and greet it each day.
practices.why: Birds are important in many Aboriginal cultures as signs of seasons and as figures in stories. Learning your local birds ties you to place.
variations: Use a bird app to confirm.

practices.name: Go slowly and gently
practices.instructions: For the first hour of your day, move slowly and gently. Walk at half your usual pace, speak quietly, put things down softly and listen to others without hurrying them. The rule of this Onda is to go slowly and gently. Notice how much rush is habit and how much is need.
practices.why: Slowness and patience are valued across many Aboriginal cultures, where relationships take time. The rule asks you to try it for an hour.

practices.name: Read the season
practices.instructions: Walk slowly for half an hour through the nearest piece of open ground. Go at a pace that lets you notice things. What is in flower, what is fruiting and what is dying back. Which birds and insects are about. Where the wind comes from and how the light falls. Say the season in your own words. Many Aboriginal peoples keep seasonal calendars of six or more seasons based on what plants and animals do.
practices.why: Aboriginal seasonal calendars read the land’s signs rather than the date. Noticing what is in flower and fruit builds a similar attention.
variations: Note one change from last week.
Look up the local Aboriginal seasons.

practices.name: Look after your place
practices.instructions: Choose one small piece of ground that you can reach every day: a garden, a verge, a creek bank, a corner of a park. Spend twenty minutes looking after it. Pick up what does not belong. Pull weeds if you know them. Water what is thirsty. Learn from it. The rule of this Onda is to look after your place.
practices.why: Caring for Country is a duty and a joy in Aboriginal cultures: the land looks after you and you look after it. Looking after one small place is the daily form.
variations: Pick up litter along a creek.
Learn the names of five plants.

practices.name: Learn one local plant
practices.instructions: Choose one native plant in your area and learn about it: its name, how it grows, when it flowers, who eats it, and how Aboriginal people have used it, from a trusted source such as an Aboriginal-authored book or website. Find one in person. Look at the leaves and the bark. Do not pick or eat anything without expert guidance.
practices.why: Aboriginal people have deep knowledge of the uses of native plants for food, tools and medicine. Learning one plant well is a respectful beginning.

practices.name: Ngapartji ngapartji
practices.instructions: Practise ngapartji ngapartji, I give you something and you give me something: reciprocal exchange. Offer someone a gift or a favour, and accept one from them. Teach a skill in return for learning one. Don’t keep score. In the Pitjantjatjara language it describes a relationship of mutual giving and learning. Sharing is a rule of this Onda.
practices.why: Ngapartji ngapartji is a Pitjantjatjara phrase for reciprocity, used in language-learning projects as the principle that learning is an exchange.
variations: Swap a skill with a neighbour.
Offer to help in return for a lesson.

practices.name: Keep the ball up
practices.instructions: Play woggabaliri, a traditional kicking game of New South Wales: a small group stand in a circle and try to keep a ball or beanbag in the air using feet, knees, heads and elbows, counting the number of hits. Count aloud. The goal is a high score together. Play with friends or children.
practices.why: Woggabaliri is a cooperative game, played by Wiradjuri and other peoples, in which the group tries to beat its own record. It is fun and requires no equipment.

practices.name: Read an Aboriginal author
practices.instructions: Read twenty minutes by an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander author: a poem, an essay, a children’s book or a chapter. Try Tyson Yunkaporta, Ellen van Neerven, Alexis Wright, Oodgeroo Noonuccal or Anita Heiss. Read slowly. Note one idea that is new to you and share it with someone.
practices.why: Aboriginal writers have produced some of Australia’s finest literature. Reading their own words is better than reading about them.
variations: Borrow a book from the library.

practices.name: Yarn under the sky
practices.instructions: After dark, sit outside with the people of your household, or on your own, and look up. Let your eyes adjust. Look at the dark spaces as well as the stars. Then talk without hurry. Tell what happened to you today as a story, with a beginning and an end, and let others tell theirs. Listen to the whole of each. Yarning is a way of sharing knowledge and keeping ties.
practices.why: Yarning is the Aboriginal English word for a relaxed, respectful conversation, a way of sharing stories and building relationships. It is slow, circular and equal.
variations: Sit around a candle or a small fire.
Tell the story of your day as a tale.
Ask an elder for a yarn.

practices.name: The emu in the sky
practices.instructions: On a clear night, find the Milky Way and look for the dark shapes in it, not the stars. In many Aboriginal cultures the great emu is seen in the dark clouds of the Milky Way, stretching from the Southern Cross towards Scorpius. Its position tells when emu eggs are ready to gather, in autumn. Find the head near the Coalsack and follow the neck and body. Share this only as publicly told.
practices.why: Aboriginal astronomy is among the oldest in the world. The Emu in the Sky is one of the best-known examples, shared publicly by Elders such as Ray Norris.

practices.name: Listen to a song
practices.instructions: Play an album or song by an Aboriginal artist: Gurrumul, Archie Roach, Kev Carmody, Yothu Yindi, Emily Wurramara or Baker Boy. Sit and listen all the way through. Notice the language, the instruments and the story. Support the artists by buying or streaming their work. Note that some artists have passed away.
practices.why: Aboriginal music ranges from the haunting voice of Gurrumul to the activism of Yothu Yindi. Listening carefully is respect.
variations: Listen to Treaty by Yothu Yindi.
Listen with a translation of the lyrics.
Share a favourite with a friend.

practices.name: Bake damper
practices.instructions: Bake damper: mix self-raising flour, a pinch of salt and enough water or milk to make a soft dough. Shape into a round, cut a cross on top and bake until golden, in a pan, an oven or on a camp stove. Eat it warm with butter and golden syrup. Damper was the bread of stockmen and travellers and is shared widely. Add wattleseed for a nutty note.
practices.why: Damper is a simple bread now loved by all Australians, and Aboriginal people have a long tradition of baking seed breads. Making it is easy and satisfying.

practices.name: Give a story for a story
practices.instructions: Swap stories with someone this evening. Offer a story from your own life or family, and invite them to share one in return. Hear theirs to the end. Ngapartji ngapartji: I give you something, you give me something. Try to listen as much as you speak, and thank them. Do not retell their story without permission.
practices.why: Story-swapping builds trust and understanding. Respect for who owns a story is a fundamental principle in Aboriginal cultures.

practices.name: A quiet end to the day
practices.instructions: End the day slowly and gently. Switch off screens, close the curtains, put things away softly, lower your voice and sit in the dark for a few breaths. Think of the people who have lived in this place before you, and wish them well. Acknowledge Country once more. Then rest.
practices.why: Closing the day with quiet thought is part of many cultures. Remembering those who came before gives it depth.
variations: Say the acknowledgement in the dark.

practices.name: A walk with an Aboriginal guide
practices.instructions: Take a tour or walk led by an Aboriginal guide in your area, learning about plants, places, history and living culture from the people themselves. Book in advance, pay the fee and listen. Ask questions with respect. Don’t take photographs where asked not to. Aboriginal-led tourism supports communities and gives the real thing.
practices.why: Aboriginal-led tours are the best way to learn about Country and culture from those who hold the knowledge. They also keep income in Aboriginal communities.
variations: Go to a bush tucker garden.

practices.name: Cook with native foods
practices.instructions: Cook a meal using Australian native ingredients bought from Aboriginal-owned suppliers: wattleseed damper, kangaroo or a vegetable stew with lemon myrtle and native pepper, a salad with finger lime pearls. Share it with friends and tell them where each ingredient comes from. Buying native foods fairly supports Aboriginal enterprise.
practices.why: Native foods were the first cuisine of Australia. Cooking with them is delicious, ecological and, when sourced fairly, supportive.
variations: Serve with a native herb tea.

immersePlan.name: Read from Sand Talk
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Tyson Yunkaporta’s 2019 book, which uses patterns drawn in the sand to explain Indigenous systems of thought. Note one idea.

immersePlan.name: Read Talking to My Country
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Stan Grant’s 2016 book, on being Wiradjuri and Australian. Note a line you want to remember.

immersePlan.name: Read from Welcome to Country
immersePlan.text: Read a section of Marcia Langton’s guide to Indigenous places and peoples. Choose a place to learn about.

immersePlan.name: Watch an episode of First Australians
immersePlan.text: Watch the first episode of Rachel Perkins’s documentary series on Aboriginal history since 1788, told through Aboriginal voices.

immersePlan.name: Watch Ten Canoes
immersePlan.text: Watch Rolf de Heer’s 2006 film made with the Yolŋu people of Arnhem Land, a story told in the Ganalbingu language.

immersePlan.name: Watch In My Blood It Runs
immersePlan.text: Watch the 2019 documentary of a ten-year-old Arrernte boy and his struggle at school. Notice what he knows that school doesn’t.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Gurrumul
immersePlan.text: Play the debut album of the blind Yolŋu singer Geoffrey Gurrumul Yunupingu, in Gumatj and English. Listen all the way through. This artist has passed away.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Charcoal Lane
immersePlan.text: Play Archie Roach’s 1990 album, including Took the Children Away. A heavy, important record. This artist has passed away.

immersePlan.name: Listen to From Little Things Big Things Grow
immersePlan.text: Play Kev Carmody and Paul Kelly’s 1991 song about the Gurindji walk-off at Wave Hill. Follow the story.

immersePlan.name: Look at Earth’s Creation
immersePlan.text: Look at Emily Kame Kngwarreye’s huge 1994 painting of the Anmatyerre country. Look for a full minute. This artist has passed away.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Yirrkala Bark Petitions
immersePlan.text: Look at the 1963 petitions painted on bark by Yolŋu leaders against mining on their land, the first Indigenous documents recognised by the Australian Parliament.

immersePlan.name: Look at Namatjira’s watercolours
immersePlan.text: Look at the desert landscapes painted by Arrernte artist Albert Namatjira in the Hermannsburg style. Pick one and describe the colours. This artist has passed away.

immersePlan.name: Taste wattleseed
immersePlan.text: Taste roasted and ground wattleseed in coffee, bread or ice cream, bought from an Aboriginal-owned supplier. It tastes of chocolate, coffee and hazelnut.

immersePlan.name: Taste a finger lime
immersePlan.text: Squeeze the pearls of a finger lime onto food, a native citrus often called lime caviar. Notice the pop.

immersePlan.name: Bake damper
immersePlan.text: Bake a simple flour-and-water bread in a pan or oven, and eat it warm with butter.

immersePlan.name: Brew lemon myrtle tea
immersePlan.text: Steep lemon myrtle leaves in hot water and drink slowly. Breathe the aroma.

immersePlan.name: Make a flower nectar drink
immersePlan.text: Steep a few blossoms of banksia or a sweetly scented flower in water if you know they are safe, or simply sip water sweetened with honey. Avoid any plants you cannot identify.

immersePlan.name: Drink water from a known source
immersePlan.text: Know where your water comes from, and drink a glass of it slowly, remembering that water is life in a dry country.

immersePlan.name: Learn about Welcome to Country
immersePlan.text: Read how Welcome to Country is performed by Traditional Owners at the start of events. Acknowledge, but don’t perform.

immersePlan.name: Show respect to an Elder
immersePlan.text: Greet an older person in your life as Aunty or Uncle if that is your custom, or with a special courtesy. Ask them for advice.

immersePlan.name: Share what you have
immersePlan.text: Share something with someone without being asked: food, a tool, an hour. What you have belongs to everyone who needs it.

immersePlan.name: Learn about Marngrook
immersePlan.text: Read about the traditional kicking game of western Victoria, thought to have influenced Australian rules football. Kick a ball with friends.

immersePlan.name: Play woggabaliri
immersePlan.text: Keep a ball in the air with feet, knees and elbows in a group, counting aloud as a team.

immersePlan.name: Play gorri
immersePlan.text: Play a target game: throw a stick or beanbag at a mark and see who is closest. Play with others and enjoy.

immersePlan.name: Mark NAIDOC Week
immersePlan.text: NAIDOC Week, in the first full week of July, celebrates Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander history, culture and achievements. Attend an event or read an Indigenous author.

immersePlan.name: Mark Reconciliation Week
immersePlan.text: From 27 May to 3 June, take one step toward reconciliation: learn a fact, read a book, speak to a neighbour.

immersePlan.name: Look up Uluru and Kata Tjuta
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the great sandstone formations, known to the Anangu as Uluru and Kata Tjuta, and read about the Anangu’s request not to climb. They are sacred places.

immersePlan.name: Practise dadirri
immersePlan.text: Dadirri is deep, quiet listening. Sit and listen to your surroundings for ten minutes.

immersePlan.name: Think about Country
immersePlan.text: Country is the land, waters, sky and all living things, to which Aboriginal people belong. Name three things that live where you live.

immersePlan.name: Practise yarning
immersePlan.text: Yarning is relaxed, respectful conversation. Spend twenty minutes in a yarn with someone with no agenda.

rules.text: Know whose Country you are on
rules.why: Learn the name of its people and say it. You are a guest.
Be still, wait and take it in. Understanding comes in its own time.
They carry what was handed down. Go to them and listen.
Take only what you need and leave it healthy for those who follow.
To family, to land, to story. You are who you are through them.
Do things with care and respect. Do not hurry the river.

read.title: Sand Talk: How Indigenous Thinking Can Save the World
read.creator: Tyson Yunkaporta
read.why: A member of the Apalech clan looks at the modern world through Aboriginal ways of knowing, with a drawing in the sand for each chapter.

read.title: Welcome to Country: A Travel Guide to Indigenous Australia
read.creator: Marcia Langton
read.why: A professor and Yiman and Bidjara woman explains culture, history, etiquette and where to go, state by state.

read.title: Talking to My Country
read.creator: Stan Grant
read.why: A Wiradjuri journalist writes about his family, his Country and what it is to be Aboriginal in Australia.

read.title: Follow the Rabbit-Proof Fence
read.creator: Doris Pilkington Garimara
read.why: The true story of her mother, who was taken from her family in 1931 and walked sixteen hundred kilometres home with two other girls.

read.title: Songlines: The Power and Promise
read.creator: Margo Neale and Lynne Kelly
read.why: How songlines hold knowledge across a continent. The first book of the First Knowledges series.

read.title: Growing Up Aboriginal in Australia
read.creator: Edited by Anita Heiss
read.why: Fifty short accounts of childhood from across the country, showing how different those lives are.

watch.title: First Australians
watch.creator: Rachel Perkins for SBS
watch.why: Seven episodes on the history of the continent since 1788 from the side of its first peoples. Made by an Arrernte and Kalkadoon director.

watch.title: Ten Canoes
watch.creator: Rolf de Heer and Peter Djigirr
watch.why: A story within a story told by the people of Ramingining in their own languages, the first feature film made that way.

watch.title: Samson and Delilah
watch.creator: Warwick Thornton
watch.why: Two teenagers leave a desert community for Alice Springs. Hard to watch, nearly wordless and tender.

watch.title: In My Blood It Runs
watch.creator: Maya Newell, made with the family of Dujuan Hoosan
watch.why: A ten-year-old Arrernte and Garrwa boy, a healer and a speaker of three languages, is failing at school.

listen.title: Gurrumul
listen.creator: Geoffrey Gurrumul Yunupingu
listen.why: A blind singer from Elcho Island with a high, clear voice, singing of his ancestors and his Country.

listen.title: Tribal Voice
listen.creator: Yothu Yindi
listen.why: Yolŋu and non-Indigenous musicians together. It carries the song Treaty, which put a broken promise on the radio.

listen.title: Charcoal Lane
listen.creator: Archie Roach
listen.why: Songs from a man taken from his family as a small child, among them his account of that day.

listen.title: From Little Things Big Things Grow
listen.creator: Kev Carmody and Paul Kelly
listen.why: The story of Vincent Lingiari and the Gurindji walk-off, told as a ballad.

art.title: Earth’s Creation
art.creator: Emily Kame Kngwarreye
art.why: Four panels six metres wide, covered in drifts of green, yellow and blue after rain. She began painting on canvas when she was nearly eighty.

art.title: The Aboriginal Memorial
art.creator: Forty-three artists of Ramingining
art.why: Two hundred painted hollow logs, one for each year of colonisation, standing as a forest for those who died defending their land. In the National Gallery of Australia.

art.title: The Yirrkala Bark Petitions
art.creator: Yolŋu clan leaders
art.why: Typed petitions to Parliament framed in painted bark that sets out the clans’ title to their land. They hang in Parliament House.

art.title: Watercolours of the western ranges
art.creator: Albert Namatjira
art.why: Ghost gums and purple hills painted by a Western Arrernte man who saw his own Country in them.

eat.title: Wattleseed
eat.creator: Roasted and ground acacia seed
eat.why: Nutty, with a taste of coffee and chocolate. Seeds were ground for bread on stones that are among the oldest in the world.

eat.title: Finger lime
eat.creator: A small native citrus
eat.why: Its flesh is made of tiny beads that burst in the mouth. From the rainforests of the east coast.

eat.title: Kangaroo
eat.creator: Lean red meat, cooked quickly
eat.why: Hunted and shared according to strict rules about who receives which part.

eat.title: Damper
eat.creator: Bread baked in the ashes
eat.why: Made long ago from the flour of native seeds, and later from wheat flour on missions and cattle stations.

drink.title: Lemon myrtle tea
drink.creator: Leaves of a rainforest tree
drink.why: Strongly lemon-scented. Buy it from an Indigenous-owned grower.

drink.title: Flower nectar water
drink.creator: Banksia or grevillea blossoms soaked in water
drink.why: A sweet drink made by steeping nectar-rich flowers.

drink.title: Water
drink.creator: From a known source
drink.why: On the driest inhabited continent, knowing where water is has always been the first knowledge.

customs.title: Welcome to Country
customs.creator: Given by Traditional Owners
customs.why: A speech, song, dance or smoking by which the people of a place welcome visitors and wish them safe passage.

customs.title: Respect for Elders
customs.creator: Aunty and Uncle
customs.why: Older people are served first, listened to and consulted before decisions are made.

customs.title: Names of those who have died
customs.creator: A period of silence
customs.why: In many communities the name and image of a person are not used after their death. Australian films and books carry a warning for this reason.

customs.title: Sharing
customs.creator: What you have belongs to your kin
customs.why: Food, money and belongings move along the lines of kinship. To keep things for yourself is poor behaviour.

games.title: Keentan
games.creator: Ball game · north-west Queensland
games.why: Two teams pass a ball, and it must be caught by a player jumping off the ground. The name means play in the Wik-Mungkan language.

games.title: Marngrook
games.creator: Ball game · western Victoria
games.why: A game of the Gunditjmara and neighbouring peoples played with a ball of possum skin, with high kicks and leaping catches.

games.title: Woggabaliri
games.creator: Ball game · New South Wales
games.why: A Wiradjuri game in which a circle of players keeps a ball in the air with feet and knees and no one wins.

games.title: Gorri
games.creator: Target game · many regions
games.why: A disc of bark is rolled along the ground and players throw at it as it passes, as practice for hunting.

festivals.title: NAIDOC Week
festivals.creator: The first full week of July
festivals.why: A week celebrating the history, culture and achievements of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, with events in every town.

festivals.title: National Reconciliation Week
festivals.creator: 27 May to 3 June
festivals.why: Between the anniversaries of the 1967 referendum and the Mabo decision. It follows National Sorry Day on 26 May.

festivals.title: Garma Festival
festivals.creator: Early August, north-east Arnhem Land
festivals.why: Four days of dance, song, art and public debate hosted by the Yolŋu on their own ground.

festivals.title: Laura Quinkan Dance Festival
festivals.creator: Every second July, Cape York
festivals.why: Communities from across the Cape gather to dance on a ground used for that purpose for a very long time.

places.title: Uluru and Kata Tjuta
places.creator: Northern Territory
places.why: The great rock and the domes beside it, owned by Anangu and returned to them in 1985. Walk around the base. The climb was closed in 2019 at the owners’ request.

places.title: Kakadu
places.creator: Northern Territory
places.why: Country of the Bininj and Mungguy, with rock paintings at Ubirr and Burrungkuy made over some twenty thousand years.

places.title: Budj Bim
places.creator: South-west Victoria
places.why: Channels, weirs and ponds built in lava flows by the Gunditjmara to farm eels, some of them 6,600 years old. A World Heritage site run by its owners.

places.title: Lake Mungo
places.creator: Willandra Lakes, New South Wales
places.why: A dry lake bed where people were laid to rest with ceremony some forty-two thousand years ago. Visit with a guide from the three Traditional Owner groups.

places.title: Brewarrina fish traps
places.creator: Barwon River, New South Wales
places.why: Stone walls and pens across half a kilometre of river, kept by the Ngemba and shared with neighbouring peoples at great gatherings.

places.title: The Aboriginal Tent Embassy
places.creator: Canberra
places.why: Set up on the lawn opposite Parliament on 26 January 1972 and still there. The longest continuous protest for Indigenous land rights in the world.

ethics.title: Respect
ethics.text: For Elders, for Country, for other people’s business.
ethics.practice: Ask before you assume you are entitled to know or to enter.

ethics.title: Responsibility
ethics.text: Rights to land come with the duty to look after it.
ethics.practice: Name one place you are responsible for and do something for it.

ethics.title: Reciprocity
ethics.text: What is given returns. Share what you have.
ethics.practice: Give something today to someone in your circle who needs it.

ethics.title: Patience
ethics.practice: Wait for one thing today without pushing.

ethics.title: Listening
ethics.practice: In one conversation today, say only a quarter of what you want to.

ethics.title: Truth-telling
ethics.text: The past has to be faced before it can be put right.
ethics.practice: Find out one hard fact about the history of the place you live.

philosophy.title: Belonging to land
philosophy.text: People do not own Country. They belong to it and are answerable to it.
philosophy.practice: What place are you answerable to?

philosophy.title: Everywhen
philosophy.text: Creation is not over. The ancestral past is present in the land and renewed by those who care for it.
philosophy.practice: Where does the past feel present to you?

philosophy.title: Knowledge in place
philosophy.text: What is known is tied to particular places and carried in story, song and walking.
philosophy.practice: What do you know that you could only have learned in one place?

philosophy.title: Kinship with everything
philosophy.text: Every person, animal, plant and place stands in a family relation to every other.
philosophy.practice: How would you treat a river if it were a relative?

philosophy.title: Kanyini
philosophy.text: A person is held by four ties: law, spirit, land and family. Cut them and the person is lost.
philosophy.practice: Which of your ties is weakest?

philosophy.title: Two-way learning
philosophy.text: Where fresh and salt water meet, both remain. Different kinds of knowledge can meet in the same way.
philosophy.practice: What have you dismissed because it was not your kind of knowledge?

philosophy.title: The right to know
philosophy.text: Not all knowledge is for everyone. Some is earned, and some belongs to others.
philosophy.practice: What are you not entitled to know?

philosophy.title: Makarrata
philosophy.text: After a wrong, the parties face each other, the truth is told and peace is made.
philosophy.practice: What struggle in your life is waiting for its coming together?

intro: People reached Australia by sea at least sixty-five thousand years ago, according to tools and ground ochre dated at a rock shelter in Arnhem Land. Their descendants spread across every part of a continent the size of Europe, from tropical coast to desert to cold southern forest. By 1788 there were several hundred nations, speaking more than two hundred and fifty languages and many more dialects. Aboriginal Australians are not one people with one culture. A Yolŋu person from Arnhem Land and a Noongar person from the south-west differ as much as a Greek and a Swede. Torres Strait Islanders, from the islands to the north, are a separate group of peoples again.

What these cultures share is a way of understanding the relation between people and land. Each group belongs to a particular Country, a word that in Aboriginal English takes in the earth, waters, sky, plants, animals and the spirits of the place. In the beginning, ancestral beings travelled across the land, forming its hills and rivers and giving each people its law, its language and its ceremonies. English calls this the Dreaming, a poor translation of words such as Tjukurpa and Jukurrpa. It is not a time that is over. The ancestors remain in the places they made, and their journeys are remembered in songs that also serve as maps.

From this follows a duty. People do not own Country so much as belong to it and care for it. They managed the land with skill, burning it in small patches to renew growth, building stone traps for fish and eels, harvesting and storing seeds and moving with the seasons. Elaborate systems of kinship set out how each person was related to every other and what each owed. Authority lay with Elders, and knowledge was passed on in stages through story, song, painting and ceremony. Much of it remains restricted to those with the right to know.

British colonisation began at Sydney in January 1788. The colonists treated the land as belonging to no one. Smallpox and other diseases killed great numbers of people, and settlers and police killed many thousands more in a frontier war that lasted into the 1930s. Survivors were pushed onto missions and reserves, where governments controlled where they lived, whom they married and whether they were paid. From about 1910 to 1970, many thousands of children were taken from their families to be raised in institutions or white homes. They are known as the Stolen Generations.

Aboriginal people never stopped resisting. A Day of Mourning was held in 1938. In 1966 Gurindji stockmen walked off a cattle station and stayed out for eight years until land was returned. A referendum in 1967 passed with more than ninety per cent in favour. In 1992 the High Court, in a case brought by Eddie Mabo of the Torres Strait, ruled that the land had not been empty and that native title could survive. The Prime Minister apologised to the Stolen Generations in 2008. In 2017 the Uluru Statement from the Heart asked for a voice, a treaty and truth-telling. A referendum on the voice failed in 2023.

About a million Australians now identify as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. Most live in towns and cities. Languages are being revived, land is being returned and Indigenous rangers care for vast areas of the continent.
This Onda takes its practices only from what Aboriginal teachers have openly shared with everyone: deep listening, acknowledging Country, reading the seasons, caring for a place and yarning.
guide.origin: The continent of Australia and its islands, home to several hundred distinct nations
guide.era: People have lived in Australia for at least 65,000 years. Aboriginal cultures are the oldest continuing cultures on Earth

figures.name: Pemulwuy
figures.bio: A Bidjigal man who led twelve years of armed resistance to the colony at Sydney. He was shot dead and his head was sent to England.

figures.name: Truganini
figures.bio: A Nuenonne woman of Tasmania who lived through the destruction of her people’s society, worked as a guide and negotiator and was long wrongly called the last of her people.

figures.name: William Cooper
figures.bio: A Yorta Yorta man who petitioned the King for representation in Parliament and organised the Day of Mourning in 1938. That year he also led a protest against the Nazi persecution of Jews.

figures.name: David Unaipon
figures.bio: A Ngarrindjeri preacher, inventor and the first Aboriginal author to be published. He appears on the fifty dollar note.

figures.name: Albert Namatjira
figures.bio: A Western Arrernte painter who became famous across Australia and was the first Aboriginal person in the Northern Territory to be granted citizenship rights.

figures.name: Vincent Lingiari
figures.bio: A Gurindji stockman who led the walk-off from Wave Hill station in 1966. In 1975 the Prime Minister poured a handful of soil into his hand as the land was returned.

figures.name: Emily Kame Kngwarreye
figures.bio: An Anmatyerr Elder from Utopia who produced some three thousand paintings in eight years and is counted among the great painters of the century.

figures.name: Oodgeroo Noonuccal
figures.bio: A poet and activist of Minjerribah. Her book We Are Going, 1964, was the first book of verse published by an Aboriginal writer.

figures.name: Charles Perkins
figures.bio: An Arrernte and Kalkadoon man who led the Freedom Ride through country towns of New South Wales in 1965 and later headed the federal Aboriginal affairs department.

figures.name: Galarrwuy Yunupingu
figures.bio: A Gumatj leader who as a young man helped draft the bark petitions and spent his life pressing for land rights and constitutional recognition.

figures.name: Miriam-Rose Ungunmerr-Baumann
figures.bio: An artist and educator from Nauiyu on the Daly River, the first fully qualified Aboriginal teacher in the Northern Territory. Senior Australian of the Year in 2021.

figures.name: Cathy Freeman
figures.bio: A Kuku Yalanji and Birri Gubba sprinter who lit the flame at the Sydney Olympics in 2000 and won the 400 metres.

history.detail: Stone axes, grindstones and ochre at Madjedbebe in Arnhem Land are the oldest evidence so far of people in Australia.
A woman is cremated and a man buried with red ochre on the shore of a lake in what is now New South Wales. They are among the oldest ritual burials known.
The Gunditjmara begin building channels and traps to farm eels, among the oldest aquaculture systems in the world.
Fishermen from Makassar sail each year to Arnhem Land for sea cucumber and trade with the Yolŋu, who take up words, pipes and sails from them.
The First Fleet lands at Sydney Cove on Gadigal land. Smallpox kills perhaps half the people of the region the following year.
Fighting and massacres follow the spread of settlement. The last officially sanctioned killings are at Coniston in 1928.
Governments remove Aboriginal children from their families under laws of protection and assimilation.
On the 150th anniversary of the landing, Aboriginal leaders meet in Sydney to demand citizenship and equality.
The Yolŋu send bark petitions against a mine on their land. Students ride through New South Wales to expose segregation. The Gurindji walk off Wave Hill.
Australians vote to count Aboriginal people in the census and let the national parliament make laws for them.
The Tent Embassy is raised in Canberra. The Aboriginal flag, designed by Harold Thomas, flies there. A land rights law for the Northern Territory passes in 1976.
The High Court rejects the doctrine that Australia belonged to no one in 1788 and recognises native title.
Prime Minister Kevin Rudd apologises in Parliament to the Stolen Generations.

history.what: The Uluru Statement and the referendum
history.detail: Delegates from across the country ask for a voice to Parliament, treaty and truth. The proposal for a voice is defeated at a referendum on 14 October 2023.

concepts.detail: Country includes everything within it and is addressed as a person. People speak to it, sing to it, worry about it and grieve for it.
The ancestral beings made the world and set down the law. Their actions are held in story and ceremony and fixed in the features of the land.
Each song cycle follows an ancestor’s route from place to place. To know the song is to know the way, the water and the law of each stretch.
Systems of sections and skin names give each person a known relationship, with its duties and its manners, to every other person and to the natural world.
Looking after land is a religious, legal and practical duty. Fire, harvest and ceremony all keep Country healthy.

concepts.text: Given at the beginning and unchanged.
concepts.detail: Aboriginal law covers marriage, land, ceremony, trade and punishment. It is held by senior men and women and taught over a lifetime.
Some knowledge belongs only to men or to women, to particular clans or to the initiated. Respecting this is basic courtesy.
Unlike in New Zealand or North America, Britain signed no treaty with the peoples of Australia. Their claim to the land was never given up.
Stories from several coasts describe the sea rising at the end of the last ice age, some ten thousand years ago, and geologists have matched them to drowned shorelines.

facts.text: The Aboriginal flag is black for the people, red for the earth and yellow for the sun. Harold Thomas, a Luritja man, designed it in 1971.
Of more than 250 languages spoken in 1788, about 120 are still spoken and only a dozen or so are being learned by children as a first language.
Ground-edge axes found in northern Australia are the oldest in the world.
Indigenous Protected Areas make up about half of Australia’s national reserve system on land.
The name kangaroo comes from gangurru in the Guugu Yimithirr language of north Queensland, written down by James Cook’s party in 1770.
The census of 2021 counted 812,728 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. The official estimate of the true number is about 984,000.

sensitivity.note: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this Onda contains the names of people who have died. It was written by outsiders from published sources and uses only what Aboriginal teachers have shared publicly. It should be reviewed by Aboriginal readers.
requiredCaveats: There is no single Aboriginal culture. Each word here belongs to a particular language and people, who are named, and customs differ from one Country to the next.
Ceremonies, sacred sites, designs and much traditional knowledge are restricted. Nothing in this Onda asks you to copy a ceremony, paint in an Aboriginal style or play the yidaki.
Colonisation is not in the past. Its effects on health, land, language and family are still being lived, and telling the truth about it is part of respect.
Buy art, food and tours from Aboriginal-owned businesses, and check that artists have been paid fairly.
